detail.abstract: We embed a ChatGPT-based AI detector in a laboratory experiment to test whether participants are willing to pay more to collaborate with AI than with human peers to accurately detect the proportion of AI-generated parts in deepfake news articles. Task difficulty varies with the model used to generate the articles (GPT-2 vs. GPT-4o). We find that participants' willingness to pay (WTP) for the AI detector exceeds that to collaborate with human peers, even though the AI detector does not provide better assistance and, in fact, humans do better than AI in for GPT-4o generated news. WTP for AI or peer collaboration does not rise with task difficulty. These patterns point to over-reliance on AI and raise concerns about the spread of deepfakes. The study improves understanding of human-AI interaction and informs safeguards for deepfake detection in the era of generative AI (GAI).

title: Robotic Versus Traditional Capital Complementarity and Economic Growth in the Era of Full Automation
affiliations: University of Milan - Department of Business Policy and Economics, Vienna University of Economics and Business - Department of Economics and Université Paris VIII Vincennes-Saint-Denis

detail.title: Robotic Versus Traditional Capital Complementarity and Economic Growth in the Era of Full Automation
detail.abstract: How will the widespread deployment of automation technologies such as industrial robots and artificial intelligence (AI) affect long-run economic performance? To address this question, we develop a model of economic growth for a fully automated economy in which output is produced with only two forms of capital: "traditional capital" (assembly lines, machines, etc.) and "robotic capital" (industrial robots, AI, etc.). In our setting, human labor is no longer competitive, and the central questions become how investment should be allocated across the two types of capital and how the degree of substitutability between them affects longterm economic growth. Using a two-level nested CES production structure (with no further assumptions), we characterize the competitive balanced growth path and the range of feasible long-run growth rates that a fully automated economy can attain. We show that the case of full automation can be consistent with the growth expectations of techno-optimists and the dynamics of economic growth along a balanced growth path depend on preference parameters, depreciation, and the degree of substitutability between robotic and traditional capital in both production and investment decisions. Our framework contributes to the debate on the economic consequences of automation and the extent to which this future is shaped by the underlying forces that determine the accumulation of traditional capital versus robotic capital.

title:
Teleology Reversed

Cause, Story, and the Shape of Human Error
affiliations: Independent

detail.title:
Teleology Reversed

Cause, Story, and the Shape of Human Error
detail.abstract:
This essay argues that intention is a teleological construct: a projection of purpose onto behavior born from first-person awareness of willing. It is not an ontic primitive but an epistemic shorthand that redescribes causal histories from the vantage of an anticipated end, it belongs to our explanatory stance, not to the fabric of being. A single structural feature of human consciousness - the asymmetry between vivid awareness of will and relative ignorance of its causes - underlies a wide family of distortions: religious teleology, ideological fanaticism, self-deception, and our chronic misreading of other people’s words. Because we feel intention from the inside and do not see its genealogy, we project purpose onto world, self, institutions, and history. Teleology in this sense is not a harmless metaphor, it is a systematic time-reversal error in explanation. It treats downstream functions as upstream intentions, and then builds entire moral and political scripts on that inversion.

Drawing on classical rationalist insights (Spinoza, Leibniz) and contemporary work in cognitive science, social theory, and the philosophy of language, I develop four linked theses. First, teleological perception is a natural default of consciousness and language, not a local superstition. Second, religion and religion-like systems (nationalisms, party ideologies, brand cults) are late-stage packages that stabilize pre-existing teleological habits, they are amplifiers, not generators. Third, our self-understanding and interpersonal speech are shaped by the same bias: we mistake the comfort of a narrative for knowledge of cause, and search for “true intention” where only causal webs exist. Finally, I outline an alternative: a life and a polity ordered by cause before story - the principle that every phenomenon, including belief, must be understood through sufficient causes before we elevate it to meaning or purpose. This is not a call to abolish meaning, but to relocate it: from first cause to human result. On this basis, reason becomes not cold detachment but the disciplined practice of re-aligning explanation with time.

title: Synthetic Media in Modern Banking: Accountability, Governance and Consumer Protection in the Age of Digital Fraud
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Synthetic Media in Modern Banking: Accountability, Governance and Consumer Protection in the Age of Digital Fraud
detail.abstract: The emergence of artificial intelligence (AI)-generated or manipulated content, such as voice cloning, generative text, and deepfakes, has revolutionized digital communications and the financial services industry. AI technologies improve productivity, automate decision-making, and increase accessibility in contemporary banking. However, they also create previously unheard-of opportunities for financial fraud, identity theft, and deceit. With an emphasis on accountability, governance, and consumer protection, this paper examines the legal and regulatory ramifications of AI-enabled fraud in financial institutions. It looks at the dual aspect of liability: is the bank, the consumer, the technology provider, or the regulator accountable when synthetic media makes fraud easier? Drawing on Nigerian and foreign frameworks, the paper evaluates the effectiveness of laws like Nigeria's Cybercrimes (Prohibition, Prevention, etc.) by using frameworks from both Nigeria and other countries, the consumer protection guidelines of the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN), and comparative tools such as the EU AI Act 2024, the operational resilience strategy of the UK Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), and the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) guidelines on AI impersonation in the United States. In order to address synthetic media risks in banking, the paper's conclusion suggests an integrated accountability model that unifies digital governance, fortifies consumer protection, and fosters international collaboration.

title: The Double Burden: The Impact of School Closures on Labor Force Participation of Mothers
affiliations: University of Wuppertal

detail.title: The Double Burden: The Impact of School Closures on Labor Force Participation of Mothers
detail.abstract: This paper examines the impact of school closures on the labor supply of women with school-aged children in Mexico during the COVID-19 pandemic. Based on a DiD approach that uses women with nursery-aged children as a control group, I find that school closures led to a 3% decrease in labor force participation and employment, along with a half-an-hour reduction in weekly working hours. Domestic work increases by nearly 1.3 hours. These effects are particularly pronounced for women with medium education, those in informal employment, and those working in sectors without flexible remote work options. There are differentials in the labor supply of single mothers and no differentials for mothers with access to informal childcare. Importantly, women’s labor force participation returns to pre-closure levels once schools re-open.
